findings.quote: CpG methylation of mitochondrial DNA is absent or below 2% once the DNA is linearized before conversion, and higher values are an artifact
findings.source: Hong et al. 2013, Mol Cell Biol 33:2683, doi:10.1128/MCB.00220-13; Liu et al. 2016, Sci Rep 6:23421, doi:10.1038/srep23421; Mechta et al. 2017, Front Genet 8:166, doi:10.3389/fgene.2017.00166; Owa et al. 2018, PLoS ONE 13:e0192722, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0192722
findings.evidence: Not every one of the four papers says this, and three of them say it less firmly. Liu, Abstract: "We found that the average methylation levels of nine regions were all less than 2% for both sample types." Liu, section "Human mitochondrial genome DNA methylation profiling": "other than two CpG sites within D-loop region, the methylation levels of the rest of the 81 CpG sites were all less than 3%. The mean methylation levels at CpG16 site (nt544) and CpG429 site (nt16411) within D-loop region were relatively high and obviously prominent, which were both about 5% in blood samples and saliva samples." Mechta, Abstract: "... prior to bisulfite sequencing decreased cytosine unconversion rate to <1.5% at all the investigated regions: D-loop, tRNA-F+12S, 16S, ND5 and CYTB, suggesting that mtDNA supercoiled structure blocks the access to bisulfite conversion."; Conclusion: "We identified a likely source of an artifact as a cause for the overestimation of cytosine methylation in mtDNA". Owa, Abstract: "Bisulfite-seq deep sequencing of linearized, gel-purified human mtDNA detected 9.4%-14.8% brCs for 9 CpG sites in ND1 gene. However, because all these brCs were associated with adjacent non-CpG brCs showing the same degrees of bisulfite resistance, DNA methylation in this mtDNA-encoded gene was not confirmed." (linearization alone did not remove the false signal); section "Shotgun bisulfite deep sequencing analysis of mtDNA methylation" (DNA sonicated, not cut with an enzyme): "In all mtDNA-encoded genes and lambda DNA, CpG methylation did not exceed 1.0%, except for three CpG sites in ND2, COX2, and D-Loop (Fig 6B)."; last sentence of the Discussion: "Future studies will be necessary to determine the exact levels of DNA methylation in the mitochondrial genome, which could show tissue specificity and/or affected by diseases or environmental factors." Hong (abstract only, full text not retrievable): "We found no evidence of CpG methylation at a biologically significant level in these regions of the human mitochondrial genome." The abstract names neither linearization nor a conversion artifact; the HindIII digestion and the upper value of 0.66% are known here from Liu et al. and Owa et al. only.
findings.proposed_text: most bisulfite studies that cut or fragmented the DNA before conversion find CpG methylation of mitochondrial DNA absent or at the background of the method (at most 0.66% in Hong et al., as reported by Liu et al. and Owa et al.; regional means below 2% in Liu et al., with two of 83 CpGs near 5%; at most 1.5% in Mechta et al.; below 1% at all but three CpGs in the shotgun library of sonicated DNA of Owa et al.), and Liu et al., Mechta et al. and Owa et al., not Hong et al., attribute higher values to an artifact, which they state as likely and not as proven, and which linearization alone did not remove in Owa et al. (9.4% to 14.8% at nine CpGs of one gene in linearized DNA, with the same level at the neighbouring non-CpG cytosines)

findings.quote: for bivalves one study reports methylated mitochondrial DNA in gonads of the mussel Mytilus edulis
findings.evidence: The abstract supports the clause ("Our results confirm the presence in mitochondria of methylated cytosines and adenines"), the full text limits it to antibody and restriction-enzyme assays. The sequencing, which is the only part comparable to the data of this project, found none at CpGs. Results, "Mitochondrial methylome sequencing unveil low global cytosine methylation rates": "Overall, the mapped mt-methylseq data showed very low global methylation rates along the M and F mtDNAs of these three male samples, either on CpGs (M = 0.3% and F = 0.5%) and non-CpGs (M = 0.6% and F = 0.8%). These results contrast with methylation rates observed on CpGs of nuclear DNA (10.0%; Supplementary Fig. S5) but are comparable to the rates on non-CpGs (0.9%; Supplementary Fig. S5)." and "This d-loop methylation peak reached the highest overall methylation level (12.3–24.8% on the M mtDNA, 16.4–35.5% on the F mtDNA)" at three cytosines in non-CpG contexts. Discussion: "Despite clear evidence of CpG methylation shown by MSRE and ICC results, mt-methylseq data revealed very low CCGG methylation rates (Supplementary Table S4), and only non-CpG methylation in the d-loop where one clear peak was observed in both M and F mtDNAs, at homologous positions." and "Globally, two contradictory cytosine methylation status were observed in M. edulis male germ cells." Method of the sequencing: enzymatic conversion (NEBNext Enzymatic Methyl-Seq), not bisulfite.
findings.proposed_text: for bivalves two studies sequenced mitochondrial DNA after conversion. In male gametes of one C. gigas no cytosine of the mitochondrial genome was considered methylated and 2,316 of 2,518 cytosines with fivefold coverage were fully converted (whole-genome bisulfite sequencing, lambda control 99.72% converted; Olson and Roberts 2014, Front Physiol 5:224, doi:10.3389/fphys.2014.00224). In gonads of three male mussels Mytilus edulis, enzymatic methylation sequencing of linearized DNA gave 0.3% and 0.5% at the CpGs of the two mitochondrial genomes, against 0.6% and 0.8% at their non-CpG cytosines and 10.0% at nuclear CpGs, with one peak of 12.3% to 35.5% at three non-CpG cytosines of the control region; an antibody and methylation-sensitive restriction enzymes indicated methylated cytosines in mitochondria in the same study, which reports the two results as contradictory

findings.where: issues.md, I-01, same point, sentence beginning "Methylation at the non-CpG cytosines of the mitochondrial genome, which the alignments hold"
findings.quote: would settle the cause: equal rates at CpG and non-CpG cytosines mean non-conversion
findings.source: no source is cited at this sentence; the test is that of Owa et al. 2018, PLoS ONE 13:e0192722, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0192722
findings.evidence: Owa et al. state the test with its assumption and as a presumption, Discussion: "Evaluation of bisulfite conversion efficiency of mtDNA using brC levels at non-CpG sites is depending on an assumption that mtDNA methylation is specific to CpG sites." and "we presume that our deep sequencing detection of cytosine methylation with equal strength for all CpG and non-CpG sites in human ND1 gene was likely reflecting false-positive artifact rather than a biological phenomenon". The assumption is contested in work after 2018 that used controls for the artifact: Patil et al. 2019, Abstract: "The data show that mitochondrial genomes are extensively methylated predominantly at non-CpG sites."; Dou et al. 2019, Results: "the H strand had an average methylation of only 8%, whereas the L strand was 23% methylated", with "Unmethylated lambda DNA was used as a spike-in control, and two PCR products of mtDNA were used as an unmethylated mtDNA negative control to ensure bisulfite conversion efficiency". Both are disputed (Guitton, Nido and Tzoulis 2022; Guitton et al. 2022; Yin, Gong and Mao 2026). In the mussel, Leroux et al. report one peak at non-CpG cytosines of the control region with enzymatic conversion.
findings.proposed_text: would narrow the cause: equal rates at CpG and non-CpG cytosines are what incomplete conversion gives and what Owa et al. take as its sign, and an excess confined to CpGs would point to CpG methylation or to reads from methylated nuclear copies. The test assumes, as Owa et al. say, that mitochondrial methylation, if it exists, is specific to CpGs. Two studies report methylation of non-CpG cytosines in mammalian mitochondria, mostly on one strand (Patil et al. 2019, Nucleic Acids Res 47:10072, doi:10.1093/nar/gkz762; Dou et al. 2019, Genome Res 29:1622, doi:10.1101/gr.234021.117), which others attribute to the same artifacts (Guitton, Nido and Tzoulis 2022, Nucleic Acids Res 50:9190, doi:10.1093/nar/gkac701; Yin, Gong and Mao 2026, Epigenetics Chromatin 19:44, doi:10.1186/s13072-026-00692-z), so equal rates would make non-conversion the likely cause without proving it; the comparison is best made for each strand and along the molecule

sources.citation: Hong EE, Okitsu CY, Smith AD, Hsieh CL 2013. Regionally specific and genome-wide analyses conclusively demonstrate the absence of CpG methylation in human mitochondrial DNA. Mol Cell Biol 33:2683-2690, doi:10.1128/MCB.00220-13

sources.citation: Liu B, Du Q, Chen L, Fu G, Li S, Fu L, Zhang X, Ma C, Bin C 2016. CpG methylation patterns of human mitochondrial DNA. Sci Rep 6:23421, doi:10.1038/srep23421
sources.note: Human blood (154 persons), saliva (24) and lung (7); bisulfite pyrosequencing and mass spectrometry of amplicons, not WGBS. Supports: circular DNA is converted less completely than DNA cut with BamHI; the effect is present in blood and lung and absent in saliva; it differs between the four regions tested; regional means after BamHI are below 2%. Limits: two of 83 CpGs are near 5% after linearization and 81 are below 3%; the authors restrict the rule ("at least for blood samples") and say of other studies that their values "might be overestimated"; saliva differed from blood in the extraction method and in the amount of DNA, which the authors give as possible reasons.

sources.citation: Mechta M, Ingerslev LR, Fabre O, Picard M, Barrès R 2017. Evidence suggesting absence of mitochondrial DNA methylation. Front Genet 8:166, doi:10.3389/fgene.2017.00166
sources.note: Human cell lines (HEK293, SKOV3, myotubes) and mouse skeletal muscle; targeted bisulfite sequencing and bisulfite sequencing of sonicated purified mitochondrial DNA. Supports: after BamHI digestion at most 1.5% at five regions; undigested DNA up to 32.3% in the D-loop; values differ between regions and cell types. The authors hedge throughout ("suggesting", "a likely source of an artifact", title "Evidence suggesting absence"). In the sonicated whole-mitochondrial library unconverted cytosines remained, more at positions of low coverage, so sonication did not remove the artifact there. The authors tested and excluded nuclear copies of mitochondrial DNA as the source in their preparations.

sources.citation: Owa C, Poulin M, Yan L, Shioda T 2018. Technical adequacy of bisulfite sequencing and pyrosequencing for detection of mitochondrial DNA methylation: sources and avoidance of false-positive detection. PLoS ONE 13:e0192722, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0192722
sources.note: Human iPS cells and mouse liver; pyrosequencing, amplicon sequencing and one shotgun bisulfite library of sonicated mitochondrial DNA with lambda DNA. Supports: closed circular DNA resists conversion (assays without linearization failed quality control); the effect differs between genes (ND1 against CYTB); shotgun values are at background (CpG up to 0.65%, non-CpG 0.50% to 0.55%, lambda 0.55% to 0.60%). Does not support "below 2% once linearized" as a rule: linearized, gel-purified DNA still gave about 30% and 9% at two CpGs with an unselective primer and 9.4% to 14.8% at nine CpGs in amplicon sequencing, which the authors attribute to local incomplete conversion. Local unevenness is described for the targeted assays; the shotgun library showed "No apparent regional bias". The authors leave the exact level open and name contamination by nuclear copies as an alternative for the low CpG signal.

"However, the existence of methylation in the mammalian mtDNA remains the subject of debate"; most recent studies report very low or no methylation, "at least three studies contradict this conclusion"; "In conclusion, while our reanalysis does not provide proof of the absence of methylation in mtDNA, we prove that the results by Patil et al. claiming a widespread mtDNA methylation are invalid". It names a second technical cause of apparent mitochondrial methylation besides the topology of the molecule: the loss of converted cytosine-rich fragments during bisulfite treatment (the mechanism of Olova et al.), which leaves reads from cytosine-rich regions under-represented and apparently fully methylated at all cytosines, and which a sonication step worsens.

result.notes:
Count: 30 statements that rest on published sources; 13 supported as worded, 16 not supported as worded (15 findings, the first covering two statements), 1 not checkable. No bibliographic error: all nine DOIs resolve at Crossref to the cited work, and authors, year, journal, volume and first page or article number agree (Crossref lacks the article number of Ji et al., Europe PMC gives 341). The only quotation (Olova et al.) is verbatim. No number taken from a source is misread. All 58 excerpts I rely on were checked by script to occur verbatim in the retrieved texts.

Answers to the particular points. (a) The four papers do not each say it. Hong et al. (abstract only) report the absence of CpG methylation and nothing on an artifact. Liu et al. and Mechta et al. support the rule for their regions, with reserve, and Liu et al. report two CpGs near 5% after linearization. Owa et al. show that linearization is needed and not sufficient. In mammals the low level at CpGs is the majority finding, also in work after 2018 that I read in the abstract (Matsuda et al. 2018, Sci Rep 8:5801; Bicci et al. 2021, Nucleic Acids Res 49:12757; Goldsmith et al. 2021, Sci Rep 11:8032), but the matter is not closed: Patil et al. 2019 and Dou et al. 2019 report real methylation, mainly at non-CpG cytosines and with controls, both contested, and Guitton et al. 2022 confirm one CpG at 5.5%. (b) Leroux et al. is open access. The methylation it reports rests on an antibody and on restriction enzymes; its sequencing (enzymatic conversion, SwaI linearization, lambda control, three of eight libraries kept) gives 0.3% and 0.5% at mitochondrial CpGs. It controlled for the artifact, and its sequencing supports the expectation instead of contradicting it. (c) Quotation verbatim; replicates statement supported by the main text; the correction replaces Additional file 3 only. (d) Yes for Pfu Turbo Cx, not for Kapa HiFi Uracil+; Arabidopsis; read coverage, not methylation level. (e) Lea et al. say so for one baboon RRBS data set, with \"seem to\". (f) It is the log's own reading; Olova et al. report largest differences at intermediate methylation and dependence on the region, and contradict the clause that non-conversion is left unchanged. (g) The test is the one Owa et al. recommend, under an assumption they state; it narrows the cause and does not settle it.

The most important omission is Olson and Roberts 2014 (Front Physiol 5:224), on this species: mitochondrial genome unmethylated in WGBS of male gametes. With the full text of Leroux et al. it turns \"not established for this species\" into limited direct support, in germ cells and gonad, not gill. The first check searched abstracts for the phrase \"mitochondrial DNA methylation\" and so missed it; the log cites another work of the same authors (a preprint) in I-49.

Works not cited that support the inference of I-01 better than the four cited, because they are WGBS libraries: Zhou et al. 2019, Morrison et al. 2021 and Yin, Gong and Mao 2026. All three tie apparent mitochondrial methylation to the absence of fragmentation before bisulfite conversion, as in post-bisulfite kits. Whether the two sequencing projects used such a kit, and whether they fragmented the DNA first, I did not establish; it is the first thing to ask of the provider records. Two consequences for the log outside my scope: the E. coli spike-in values asked for in I-49 will inform nuclear conversion (item 2) and cannot settle the mitochondrial difference of I-01, since a linear control does not show the conversion of circular DNA; and Guitton et al. 2022 show that with the nuclear genome in the reference mitochondrial reads are lost to nuclear copies, which bears on the coverage ratios of I-01.

Sentences of the scope that I did not count because they rest on the project data or on the log's own reasoning: \"Two more features of the data fit incomplete conversion\", \"so their mitochondrial DNA was converted as completely as their nuclear DNA\", \"On this reading the two projects differ ...\", \"It cannot be read as an effect of heat on mitochondrial DNA\". They are consistent with the sources read.

findings.quote: The first sentence misstates its source. In the reads of the strand that carries the cytosine, a C-to-T variant cannot be told from an unmethylated cytosine, and Bismark counts it as unmethylated; the reads of the opposite strand show an A in place of a G and identify the variant, which is the principle of Bis-SNP (Liu et al. 2012, read in full) and of the BS-Snper step of Venkataraman et al. 2022.
findings.source: Liu et al. 2012, Genome Biol 13:R61, doi:10.1186/gb-2012-13-7-r61
findings.evidence: Background of Liu et al.: "true (evolutionary) C>T SNPs in the sample cannot be distinguished from C>T substitutions that are caused by bisulfite conversion, and can thus be misidentified as unmethylated Cs". The sentence of 2026-11-18 paraphrases this and omits what follows, so 'misstates' is too strong. The solution is stated for one kind of library: "A key property of some bisulfite-related protocols is that G nucleotides on the strand opposing a C are not affected by conversion. ... Non-directional protocols (those that also result in G>A substitutions) have been used [17], but have not been widely adopted. Figure 1 illustrates the directional protocol, where approximately half the reads at a given cytosine position (those mapping to the 'C-strand') can be used for methylation quantification but cannot distinguish C>T SNPs. The other half (those mapping to the 'G-strand' ...) yield no methylation information but can be used to identify C>T SNPs." Conclusions: "The directional nature of the Illumina protocol allows for analysis of DNA methylation and the identification of a SNP at the same position". This project: both alignment runs used --non_directional (07_documentation/upstream_processing/README.md), and in each of the 22 reports of 08_archive/data/PE_reports/ the four strands hold 24.8% to 25.2% of the uniquely aligned pairs. Bismark documentation (docs, usage/alignment.md and usage/methylation-extraction.md): "FLAG (this flag tries to take the strand a bisulfite read originated from into account ...)"; "Bismark swaps those bits for CTOT/CTOB pairs in non-directional output". BS-Snper source (sam_funcs.c, line 608) puts a read on the Watson strand when "(record->r12 == 1 && record->strand == '+') || (record->r12 == 2 && record->strand == '-')", that is from the FLAG bits. Venkataraman et al. 2022, who also aligned with --non_directional: BS-Snper "takes into consideration nucleotide identity on the opposite strand: a thymine paired with an adenine indicates a C- > T SNP"; such variants "would be interpreted by Bismark as an unmethylated cytosine". The rest of the correction is supported.
findings.proposed_text: The first sentence gives half of what its source says. Liu et al. 2012 name the problem in nearly those words, such variants "cannot be distinguished from C>T substitutions that are caused by bisulfite conversion, and can thus be misidentified as unmethylated Cs", and then show how it is solved in a directional library: the reads of the strand that carries the cytosine cannot tell a C-to-T variant from an unmethylated cytosine, and Bismark counts it as unmethylated; the reads of the opposite strand show an A in place of a G and identify the variant. That is the principle of Bis-SNP (Liu et al. 2012, read in full) and of the BS-Snper step of Venkataraman et al. 2022. Liu et al. state it for directional libraries and note that non-directional protocols "also result in G>A substitutions". The libraries of this project are non-directional (both alignment runs used `--non_directional`, and in each of the 22 alignment reports the four strands hold 24.8% to 25.2% of the uniquely aligned pairs; `08_archive/data/PE_reports/`), so the distinction needs the strand of origin of each read pair. Bismark encodes it in the FLAG field of its alignments, and BS-Snper assigns reads to the two strands from that field (Bismark documentation and BS-Snper source code, read on 2026-11-19); Bis-SNP was written for the directional protocol.

missing_counter_evidence.what_it_says: A review with a simulation, written for invertebrate methylomes (honey bee against human). "MethylKit uses logistic regression for DML/DMR detection which can induce type 1 error inflation". Simulation of 1,000 CpGs, two groups, by default 10 samples per group, 10x coverage and a standard deviation of methylation among individuals of 0.1, at the 5% level: "With the exception of Fisher's exact test and logistic regression, all methods tend to have low type I error rate"; for those two "their type I errors increased rapidly to as much as 20%" as coverage and variation among individuals rose; "Among the six tools that control type I errors well, RADMeth, DSS-general and MethylSig performed similarly with higher powers and AUCs". It supports the first statement with an independent simulation. For the second it is published evidence that the general-design model of DSS holds the 5% level in a two-group simulation; it does not test the far tail of the p-values on which item 7 turns, nor a design with a covariate.

That speaks for the level of the DSS model at 5%; it does not test the far tail of the p-values on which item 7 turns.

result.notes:
Result on the five points set for refutation. (a) Wreczycka et al.: 'best accuracy overall', 'lowest specificity', 'similar results to DSS' and the chi-squared test as 'a good compromise' are verbatim and in context, in the article and in the preprint of 9 August 2017. Three things do not hold as worded. The article's code, which the article itself names, called CpGs at q < 0.01 and a difference above 5 points, so 'without a difference threshold' is wrong. The article puts the chi-squared test with the correction forward in three places, one of them in the Conclusions as 'A good alternative ... This method has high sensitivity without sacrificing too much for specificity', so 'does not recommend one test' and 'recommends was wrong' go too far the other way. And the article calls the specificity of that test 'similar' to DSS and limma, so the contrast of 5% to 7% against 1.5% is the audit's reading of the figure. The percentages are clearly labelled as measurements; measured again from the PDF image and from uncompressed figures of the code repository they are 29% to 32%, 4.6% to 6.5%, 0.8% to 1.3% and at most 1.0%. (b) Park and Wu: the four type I errors, the per-CpG dispersion, the bounds, the normal reference and the absence of a returned methylation difference (DSS guide 2.60.0) are confirmed; the authors call the bounds 'a type of shrinkage'. (c) Venkataraman et al. 2022: all confirmed (MN with Chisq, 50%, 315 of 1,599, eight animals, 'sibling oysters'). (d) The vignette's first example uses the default model with 25 points and q < 0.01, but its only example with a covariate, and that of the help page, use overdispersion='MN' with test='Chisq'; since the draft's model has a covariate and the author now states that the correction was left out on purpose, the sentence 'The draft's settings are those of the methylKit vignette' needs that qualifier. (e) Liu et al.: the strand principle is right and is stated for directional libraries; the libraries here are non-directional.

Two findings lie outside the passages named to me and are marked so: lines 185 to 191 of the header of dml_sensitivity.R (still credit the general-design model of DSS with sharing information) and the last column of the I-06 row of the corrections table. If the corrections are applied, the corrections table of issues.md needs rows for them.
